recQOLj1bGHrs7YCW.Bio: Michelle Lundquist describes herself as a folk herbalist, gardener and homemaker with a passion for plants and their ability to heal. She has studied and actively worked with herbs since 2013, drawing most of her knowledge from hands on experience and mentors of the wise woman tradition, and a do it yourself spirit runs through her work as she encourages people to take their wellbeing into their own hands. She hosted more than eighty episodes of The Healing Home podcast as a kitchen witch, homemaker and folk herbalist, and now co-hosts Symbolic Studies with her husband Mario Garza.
recQOLj1bGHrs7YCW.Name: Michelle Lundquist

fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Spring Seeds and the Lie of the Future Self", "body": "Chance opens on Pi Day with a planting metaphor and returns to it in the outro: the present and the future are not separate, so postponing health, in ourselves or in our animals, only hands the problem to a later self. He ties this to the non-linear time he had been sitting with in the Dune series and in the film Arrival, which Christopher Gardner, Topher, recommended. His closing claim is stated plainly, that your future self will feel a progressed version of whatever you feel right now, which is why he wanted this conversation in early spring rather than later."}, {"title": "Carl, the Cat Who Made Michelle an Herbalist", "body": "Michelle Lundquist traces her path back to her cat Carl, who passed the previous May at eighteen and whose photo sits on her desk. She was an herbal apprentice interning at an herb shop, drawn to a book there about herbs for animals, and says the first tincture she ever made was for him, a bottle she named the No More Coughs Meowzer Tincture and still keeps on her altar. She describes Carl as a needs cat whose flare ups tracked seasonal change, and says he taught her about plants, returning again and again to a rosemary bush in the garden that she read as a message."}, {"title": "Learning the Language Pets Already Speak", "body": "Both frame attention as the actual practice. Chance argues that a filter put up in one part of life operates everywhere, and that people underestimate pets, who in his view comprehend spoken English about as well as a small child. He recounts animal communicator Catherine O'Shea, a guest on Michelle's show The Healing Home, reading his dog Mango cold and immediately naming water as the dog's priority, with his wife Jenny watching in the chat. Michelle offers what she calls story medicine, learning an animal's history and patterns the way you would your own, pointing to Gandalf still hiding from Chance's mother years after a frightening emergency."}, {"title": "Matthew Wood's Six Tissue States as a Reading Frame", "body": "The centerpiece is a model Michelle credits to herbalist Matthew Wood, the six tissue states, drawn as a six pointed star with homeostasis at the center: hot and cold, damp and dry, tense and lax. She places it in the same family as Ayurveda's three doshas and the classical humors of Roman medicine, and mentions a Celtic version as well, calling it a symbolic language for reading a body that cannot describe itself. Her point is that an animal cannot report anything verbally, so posture, behavior and the way it moves through the world become the report, and she urges listeners to research for themselves."}, {"title": "Vibration, Mirroring, and Doing Your Own Homework", "body": "In the later stretch Michelle turns to homeopathy and flower essences, which she describes as vibration medicine, subtle and gentle rather than forceful. She says she is a believer that emotion and experience shape what eventually shows up on the physical level, in people and animals alike, and recounts weeping after a rose essence. Chance asks what happens in a multi-pet household sharing one bowl, and both answer intuitively rather than clinically. They close on mirroring, on Kyle Denton's advice to sit with one plant at a time for a whole week, and on Michelle's ebook and the Telegram chat Chance says beats a search engine."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: The mighty Michelle Lundquist of the Healing Home podcast joins InnerVerse for a heartfelt chat about taking care of cats. In this episode we discuss her initiation on the path of the herbal naturalist because of her cat's special needs, along with advice about veterinary involvement for pets, tea-time for kitties, learning your pet's story and speaking their language, recognizing the six tissue states as categories of bodily communication, flower essences, homeopathy, navigating healing crisis, and much more. These things apply to more than just cats, so tune in for a playful romp with the four legged beings closest to our hearts.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension we contemplate the mirroring between ourselves and our pets, probiotics and digestive aids, the use of comfrey, the rhythm of medicinal administration, natural remedies for fleas and ticks, the do's and don'ts with plants and oils for pets, mushrooms, CBD, and nutritional quality considerations. This extension is packed with timeless wisdom, and it's a lot of fun.
fields.Plus Chapters JSON: [{"seek": 3852, "time": "1:04:12", "title": "Back for Part Two With Tookie"}, {"seek": 3986, "time": "1:06:26", "title": "Do Pets and People Share a Biome"}, {"seek": 4077, "time": "1:07:57", "title": "Reading What Tookie Is Trying to Say"}, {"seek": 4390, "time": "1:13:10", "title": "Probiotics and Gentle Digestive Support"}, {"seek": 4533, "time": "1:15:33", "title": "Why Comfrey Is Controversial"}, {"seek": 4948, "time": "1:22:28", "title": "The On and Off Rhythm of Remedies"}, {"seek": 5078, "time": "1:24:38", "title": "Natural Approaches to Fleas and Ticks"}, {"seek": 5610, "time": "1:33:30", "title": "The Short List of Don'ts"}, {"seek": 6048, "time": "1:40:48", "title": "Ask the Community Before Google"}, {"seek": 6271, "time": "1:44:31", "title": "Bringing Mushrooms Into Pet Care"}, {"seek": 6458, "time": "1:47:38", "title": "Thoughts on CBD for Pets"}, {"seek": 6789, "time": "1:53:09", "title": "Turning to Pet Nutrition"}, {"seek": 7107, "time": "1:58:27", "title": "Read Pet Food Labels Like Your Own"}, {"seek": 7384, "time": "2:03:04", "title": "What You Spend Signals Your Worth"}, {"seek": 7596, "time": "2:06:36", "title": "The Case for Holistic Vets"}]
fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Household Mirror Runs Both Ways", "body": "Part two opens with Tookie on Chance's lap and a question about whether pets and their people share more than a mood. Michelle reads a calm, affectionate animal as a report on the whole household, since pets absorb the energy of the humans they live with the way children learn from parents. Chance pushes the idea further, describing how his dogs' stool and his own took on the same off smell while the dogs ate a particular refrigerated food, and how that stopped after the switch, which led him to suspect a shared biome and to see his avoidance of their signals as avoidance of his own."}, {"title": "Listening When a Cat Leaves a Message", "body": "Chance offers Tookie as a live case: a happy, energetic cat who sometimes leaves his droppings just outside the box and is desperate to get outside and eat grass. Michelle walks through the possibilities one at a time, from a small internal fissure to hydration and the dry tissue state, and asks careful questions about stool texture and drinking habits before suggesting anything. Her central point is behavioral, that a cat going beside the box is usually asking to be seen, and her first thoughts turn toward supporting the gut biome with pet probiotics, omega rich salmon oil and Nupro Health Nuggets."}, {"title": "Comfrey, Caution and the Rhythm of Remedies", "body": "Michelle takes on comfrey's reputation directly, explaining that the liver worries trace to the higher alkaloid content of wild comfrey and of the root, while the cultivated comfrey sold by herbal suppliers is low in it, and she has drunk comfrey infusions herself for weeks at a time. She describes ways to introduce a plant to a finicky animal, including an infusion added to food and a spritz on the paws and fur, and stresses starting slow, pausing on an alternating weekly rhythm, and rotating to marshmallow leaf rather than slippery elm because it is easier to find."}, {"title": "Fleas, Ticks and the Shorter List of Don'ts", "body": "Michelle's natural answer to fleas centers on diatomaceous earth, sometimes blended with ground lavender, cedar or lemongrass, with heavy emphasis on diluting any essential oil and never applying one straight. Chance frames the next topic as the apophatic method, where learning a few don'ts is easier than listing every safe plant. Michelle then names the plants she treats with caution, including tea tree oil, white willow bark for cats, the allium family, ephedra, pennyroyal and heavily aromatic rosemary, while noting that reliable veterinary books sometimes contradict what a quick online search says."}, {"title": "Food Grade Care and What We Think We're Worth", "body": "The closing stretch covers reishi, which Michelle saw act quickly for Carl, pet CBD and its occasional tendency to make dogs anxious, and a raw diet for cats with her caveat about too much bone. She urges reading pet food labels for natural flavors, gums, potato starch and pea protein. Chance argues that what people will spend on quality food signals what they believe they are worth, and that organic food is simply what food costs. Michelle adds that good nutrition means fewer vet bills, and recommends holistic vets as a gentler option that, in her experience, costs about the same."}]
